analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax was introduced by one representative with one cosponsor, sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax — the tax on very large inheritances — along with the gift tax and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. The estate tax applies only to estates above a large threshold, so the direct benefit of repeal would go to the heirs of the wealthiest households. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action in the two years of the 115th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. With the estate tax exemption at $5.49 million per person in 2017, only the estates of very wealthy households owe the tax at all; repeal would eliminate their tax bill entirely and let large fortunes pass between generations untaxed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes in full, effective for deaths, gifts, and transfers after enactment.
Because the tax only applies above a multi-million-dollar exemption, repeal's direct tax savings would go almost entirely to the wealthiest households.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers. Estate tax repeal would remove a revenue stream that comes from the largest estates, meaning either larger deficits or higher taxes elsewhere to make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate tax eliminates billions in annual federal revenue, which would have to be replaced by borrowing or by taxes on people who do pay.
The estate tax's purpose is to tax the largest transfers of wealth between generations; repeal removes that check entirely, with no replacement such as closing capital-gains step-up at death.

Despite the bill's name, very few family farms ever owed the estate tax, because the exemption already shields estates under roughly $11 million per couple; repeal's benefits are concentrated among the largest fortunes, not working farms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's direct benefits go to a small number of very wealthy heirs, while the cost is lost federal revenue borne by everyone else through deficits or other taxes. Even sympathetic framings — protecting family farms — are addressed by the existing exemption, which already excludes all but the very largest estates. The bill offered no offsetting savings and no middle ground such as a higher exemption.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Richard Hudson introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax remained law, so the Treasury kept the revenue and no change occurred. Because the bill had only two sponsors and no committee action, nothing was better or worse off; the heirs of large estates gained nothing, and the status quo prevailed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died untouched

for.name: Rep. Richard Hudson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and introduced it on the first day of the 115th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2017, and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew only two Republican sponsors and never reached a vote, so the record shows no broader party positioning on either side.

industries.note: Repeal would have permanently eliminated the tax on the largest inheritances, saving the heirs of multimillion-dollar estates billions. That saving would come out of federal revenue that everyone else ultimately funds through deficits or other taxes.

industries.industry: Family farms and closely held small businesses
industries.note: The bill's namesake constituency would have gained some certainty at death, though the existing multi-million-dollar exemption already shielded nearly all farms and small businesses from the tax, so the practical benefit is small.
